sentences: On a summer night, people have gathered by a pond.
They are nothing but black shadows.
Above them, in the night sky they are watching, fireworks are blooming.
This is Fireworks at Ikenohata, published in 1881 by the Japanese printmaker Kobayashi Kiyochika.
It is a woodblock print in ink and colour on paper, with an image 20.
3 centimetres high and 31.
4 wide. Ikenohata means the edge of the pond, here Shinobazu Pond in the Ueno district of Tokyo.
The print was given to The Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York in 2016.
Look first at the sky.
Fireworks open out against the dark.
Kiyochika was an artist captivated less by bright daylight than by dusk and deep night, by the moment when light seeps into darkness.
Now look at the people below.
They are printed only as black silhouettes, without faces or patterns on their clothes.
They stand together, yet each seems alone, quiet spectators rather than actors in the scene.
Find the lanterns and the willow trees by the water.
Fireworks in the sky, lanterns by the pond: different kinds of light glow at their own strengths within a single print, all achieved by inking and printing a handful of carved wooden blocks.
Kiyochika was born in Edo in 1847, into a family of minor officials serving the shogun.
When the shogunate fell in 1868, he followed the last shogun into exile in Shizuoka and got by with all kinds of odd jobs.
In 1874 he returned to the capital, now renamed Tokyo, and from 1876 he began publishing prints of its famous places.
By 1881 there were ninety-three, and twenty-five of them are night scenes.
They became known as kosenga, pictures of light.
His return coincided with the arrival of gas street lighting in Tokyo.

Other printmakers of the time celebrated trains, brick buildings and Western dress in loud colours, but Kiyochika's Tokyo is quiet and faintly melancholy, because in it the vanishing old city and the new one overlap.
His model was Hiroshige's One Hundred Famous Views of Edo.
But where Hiroshige's Edo usually sparkles under the midday sun, Kiyochika's Tokyo leans toward evening and night.
In 1881, the year this print appeared, two great fires swept through Tokyo.
Kiyochika lost his home, his studio and the neighbourhood where he was born, and the series stopped at ninety-three prints.
Step back and see it whole.
Fireworks vanish in an instant, yet the shadows of the people who watched them have stayed on this paper for more than a hundred and forty years.
Tonight, spend a moment looking at the lights outside your window.
